attacks.claim: Step 3 publishes the blog post and opens v2 to all users before step 4 advances the health gates (5xx, p95, parity). The header also schedules the blog post for launch day at 15:00, while the canary runs 48 h. Public adoption can therefore happen before the gates that are meant to protect it are checked.
attacks.evidence: "Developer blog post: same day 15:00 local" vs "3. Publish docs and blog post; open v2 to all." followed by "4. Advance gates: v2 5xx < 0.1%, p95 < 100 ms, parity monitor ≥ 99.9%."

attacks.claim: The rollback only sets the gateway weight for `/v2/*` to 0. That returns 503 to every integrated v2 client with no v1 fallback. Launch-day v1 deprecation headers and emails to 1,412 key holders cannot be recalled, and the plan does not cover them.
attacks.evidence: "Rollback: gateway route weight for `/v2/*` back to 0 (returns 503 with a link to status page); v1 unaffected." vs "From launch day, v1 responses carry `Deprecation: @1794787200` … Email to all 1,412 registered key holders on launch day"

attacks.claim: The claim that a v2 fault cannot take down v1 covers only the serving deployment and autoscaling group. v1 and v2 share the ingestion pipeline and the API gateway, so a bad ingestion or gateway change reaches v1. The artifact gives no isolation, monitoring or separate revert path for those shared components.
attacks.evidence: "v2 shares the ingestion pipeline with v1 but runs as a separate deployment and autoscaling group, so a v2 fault cannot take down v1." and "API gateway routes `/v2/*` only (v1 routes untouched)."

attacks.claim: The proposal says the guide maps every v1 field and that v2 replaces three v1 endpoints. The v2 arrivals endpoint only takes `stop_id`, so `/v1/routes/{id}/stops/{id}` and the unscoped `/v1/predictions` have no documented v2 equivalent. Those consumers have no migration path.

The launch processes personal data, including client IPs for per-IP rate limiting, `stop_id` query logs that can reveal rider travel patterns, and contact details for 1,412 key holders. The artifact states no log retention or anonymization policy, no privacy notice or lawful basis, and no retention or opt-out terms for key-holder contact data.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention, anonymization or truncation of IP and stop_id logs; privacy notice; lawful basis. "keys identify apps for rate limiting and contact" and "Reads are anonymous: no key required up to 60 requests/min per IP."

attacks.claim: The 48 h canary is limited to internal apps and three opted-in pilot partners. The 5xx and p95 gate thresholds may be judged on very little traffic, and the parity monitor has no stated owner or alert threshold.
attacks.evidence: "Canary: 5% of `/v2/*` traffic for 48 h … (traffic only from internal apps and the 3 pilot partners who opted in)." and "parity monitor ≥ 99.9%"

attacks.claim: The load test is described against origin staging. It does not say whether the 10 s CDN cache or the per-IP rate limiter was in the path, so production peak behavior through those layers, including shared-NAT 429 bursts, is unverified.
attacks.evidence: "Load test on the production-sized staging cluster: 3× current peak … 0 errors." and "anonymous 61st req/min → 429"

attacks.claim: In degraded mode the API keeps serving the last good snapshot with no maximum staleness after which it stops returning arrival times. Clients that ignore `feed_age_seconds` can present long-gone arrivals as current.
attacks.evidence: "responses keep serving the last good snapshot with `feed_age_seconds` set and `meta.degraded: true`"

attacks.claim: Anonymous v1 consumers are not emailed, and the top 20 consumers cover about 81% of traffic. The remaining roughly 19% may learn of the sunset only from response headers or the blog post, which may not reach them within the 12-month window.
attacks.evidence: "Email to all 1,412 registered key holders … Top 20 consumers by volume (≈ 81% of v1 traffic) get direct outreach" vs "Reads are anonymous: no key required"

attacks.claim: The claim that no operator or driver identifiers exist is asserted without listing the vehicle or trip fields. Real-time vehicle positions could be linked to individual operators, so the claim needs a field-level check.
attacks.evidence: "No operator/driver identifiers are present in v1 or v2." alongside "Removed vs v1: `vehicle_label` (internal fleet label, not useful to riders)"

attacks.claim: The migration guide is said to map every v1 field, but removed fields such as `vehicle_label` have no stated replacement or guidance.
attacks.evidence: "Removed vs v1: `vehicle_label`" vs "Migration guide maps every v1 field to its v2 equivalent"

attacks.claim: The public credit request differs from the required attribution text. The CC BY 4.0 attribution also has no license URI.
attacks.evidence: Blog: "Please credit \"Metro Transit\" in your app." vs Licensing: "carry the attribution text \"Contains data from Metro Transit, CC BY 4.0\"". ABSENT: link to the CC BY 4.0 license text.

attacks.claim: Rider-facing accessibility fields (`wheelchair_accessible`, `bike_rack_slots`) are published as authoritative data with no accuracy disclaimer, error-reporting path or limitation statement, although riders may rely on them for travel decisions.
attacks.evidence: "wheelchair_accessible (bool), bike_rack_slots (int or null)" with ABSENT: accuracy disclaimer or error-reporting path in the docs or blog post.
